## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>

</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# Improve the staged experiment

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a snapshot you may repair: inspect its
source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward
logic, logs, tracked metrics, and frozen run records. Do not assume that an
unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed
behavior.

Use the run's own recorded signals together — rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training-time measurements, plus the frozen evidence the
snapshot ships. A single logged number alone does not establish health or its
absence.

## Your job

If you find a defect, fix it in the staged workspace at `/workspace`. **Do not
launch training.** Do not start the experiment, in the foreground or
background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
anything you launch is wasted and scores nothing. Cheap, non-training checks
are fine.

**Do not use the network.** Do not fetch code, documentation, packages,
or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose and
repair using only what is staged locally.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Root cause**: the defect you found, and the evidence in the workspace
   (logs, metrics, code) that connects it to the observed behavior.
2. **Changes**: every file you changed and what you changed in it.
3. **Expected effect**: which recorded quantity the fix should move and in
   which direction.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## What the system will run

After you submit the report, the system restores the experiment's launch and
instrumentation pipeline — the scripts that start the run and the code that
records its measurements — to their originally staged state, deletes anything
under `runs/`, and re-runs the experiment once in your repaired workspace as
a foreground process:

```bash
bash "$AUTORLBENCH_VERIFIER/resources/replay.sh"
```

The scoring run is bounded: it trains exactly 30 steps, with no validation
passes and no checkpoints. It uses:

- the staged model at `/workspace/model` and the staged datasets under
  `/workspace/data`, exactly as staged — they are fixed, and their contents
  are verified by the grader
- the staged initial state: the run directory `runs/run_001` starts empty, so
  nothing you or a previous attempt left there counts

A task-specific grading script then reads **only this fresh run's** records
under `runs/run_001` and checks, deterministically and without any judge
model: that the run completed its bounded schedule with well-formed records;
that the staged assets, the restored pipeline, and the effective
configuration the run resolves all match the task's pins; and that the
measurements the run records are within the task's fixed bounds. The frozen
historical records under `logs/` are context, not scored. Do not copy, edit,
or fabricate run records, and do not replay the frozen records as a new run.
Otherwise the run scores 0.

Edits whose only effect is to change what the run records, rather than what it
computes, are considered tampering and score 0.
I’ll trace the recorded behavior through the configuration and training code, make an evidence-backed repair, and write `/workspace/report.md`. I’ll use only local files and non-training checks.

+   I inspected `scripts/train.sh`, `scripts/train_entry.py`, `scripts/run_support.py`, the composed Hydra configuration, dataset/tokenizer processing, the custom math reward, GRPO advantages, PPO-Seq-MIS loss, actor precision and optimizer handling, rollout synchronization, and the frozen records under `logs/run_001/`. Composing `math_grpo` with `launch.json`'s overrides produced **no differences** from the resolved configuration printed in `console/attempt_002.log`.
+
+   The active configuration uses 64 prompts with eight responses each, an 8192-token response cap, 1024-token prompt limit, GRPO without standard-deviation normalization, PPO-Seq-MIS with cutoff 3, fixed-cap loss normalization, bfloat16 actor/rollout computation, and AdamW at learning rate `1e-6`. Actor parameters and optimizer state use float32; the small Adam epsilon is not accompanied by nonfinite gradients or missed updates.
+
+   These are arithmetic means of the training records in `metrics.jsonl`, using equally sized early and late windows:
+
+   | Recorded quantity | Steps 1–30 | Steps 411–440 |
+   |---|---:|---:|
+   | `critic/score/mean` | 0.54544 | 0.76992 |
+   | `response_length/mean` | 6160.14 | 4009.76 |
+   | `response_length/clip_ratio` | 34.09% | 6.52% |
+   | `prompt_length/clip_ratio` | 0 | 0 |
+   | `actor/grad_norm` | 0.01184 | 0.00909 |
+   | `actor/entropy` | 0.61017 | 0.29048 |
+   | `timing_s/gen` | 100.66 s | 77.46 s |
+   | `timing_s/old_log_prob` | 6.41 s | 4.02 s |
+   | `timing_s/update_actor` | 20.13 s | 13.74 s |
+   | Step time excluding recorded validation/checkpoint time | 129.05 s | 96.14 s |
+
+   Generation dominates runtime, and the shorter responses accompany lower generation and update times. Regular-step throughput decreases from about 3131 to 2743 tokens/s as batches contain fewer tokens; this does not indicate growing wall-clock stalls. Historical validation/checkpoint work explains periodic long steps. The bounded replay omits that work, so those raw historical step-time spikes are not a suitable replay baseline. Entropy uses the configured fixed-cap aggregation and therefore partly declines with response length; it is not evidence of collapse in isolation.
+
+   `metrics.jsonl` contains contiguous steps 0–440 and no nonfinite metric values. Every `optimizer_rank_*.jsonl` contains exactly 1760 consecutive, finite updates, consistent with four minibatches per step on each of eight ranks. `training.complete.json` records step 440 and `last_exit.json` records exit code 0. The first attempt's exception was the deliberate resume probe in `run_support.py`; `resume.json` records data/controller restoration, and all eight rank audit records report restored parameter, optimizer, scheduler, and scaler hashes. Frozen checkpoint manifests have all eight model/optimizer/extra-state shards. Their tensor payloads are not included, so those historical hashes cannot be independently reverified here.
+
+   Dataset inspection found 1460 training rows with ground truths; exactly one exceeds the prompt cap, leaving the logged 1459 examples and 22 complete batches per epoch. Both validation datasets have 30 examples and no overlong prompts. The actor and rollout consume the same templated prompt tokens. The custom reward is explicitly selected even though training `data_source` is empty. It requires one `</think>` and a correct boxed final answer. Re-evaluating the three frozen samples reproduced their rewards and formatting flags: the unfinished step-0/440 samples receive zero, and the completed step-200 answer, 70, receives one. Their apparently over-cap validation `response_length` values include prompt tokens in `_validate`; the unfinished outputs retokenize to 8192 response tokens. This label ambiguity does not change generation or training, and changing only its reporting would be inappropriate here.
+
+   Held-out mean reward at 32 samples also improves: AIME 2024 rises from 0.228125 to 0.286458 and AIME 2025 from 0.191667 to 0.245833. These are separate from training reward and from best-of-32 accuracy. The frozen samples and validation improvements support the reward trend rather than a claim based only on training reward.
+
+   **Parity limitation:** During steps 1–30, mean absolute token log-probability disagreement averages 0.012616 nats, sequence ESS fraction averages 0.05432, and the MIS rejected-sequence fraction averages 5.19%. At step 1 the median sequence log ratio is -2.898. Thus small token differences accumulate materially over thousands of tokens. `parity_record.json` preserves a much larger individual observation at step 326: actor log probability -18.81250 versus rollout -1.26402, a 17.54848-nat difference. This must not be dismissed, but it is not sufficient evidence of a particular implementation failure: the file explicitly disclaims exact decode replay and contains no matching input tensors or weights. The discrepancy exists before optimizer updates; `ray_trainer.py` computes parity before `update_actor`, and `core_algos.py` actually uses the recorded sequence ratios for MIS weighting. Meanwhile rewards, completion rates, finite optimization, and runtime improve. A proposed stale-prefix-cache explanation was ruled out by a non-training local-runtime check: the synchronous `LLM.sleep(level=1)` wrapper calls scheduler prefix-cache reset before sleeping. No probability values or measurements were overwritten to conceal disagreement.
+
+2. **Changes**
+
+   - Added `/workspace/report.md`, this assessment. This is the only workspace file changed.
+
+   All source, configuration, launch/instrumentation scripts, staged model and datasets, and frozen records remain unchanged. No `runs/` directory was created.
+
+3. **Expected effect and verification limits**
+
+   There is no corrective computation change, so **no recorded quantity is intentionally shifted**. The fresh bounded run should retain finite updates, improving training reward, and declining truncation/response length; the historical first-30-step means above provide context, not guaranteed replay values or inferred grading thresholds. Its validation-free start also differs from the historical validation/resume sequence. No unsupported parity improvement is claimed.
+
+   Cheap checks passed: launch-shell syntax; full configuration comparison; local dataset/tokenizer and frozen-sample reward checks; record continuity and optimizer progression; CPU-only GRPO grouping under reordering; PPO-Seq-MIS identity/cutoff behavior; and fixed-cap loss equivalence across uneven microbatches. Cache lifecycle was checked using inert scheduler/executor doubles, without initializing an inference engine. No model training or experiment launch was performed, and no network access or package downloads were used.
